# Storyboard: Chapter 6, The Snake in the Stones

*Generated by `tools/storyboard.mjs` from `app/story/ch06.js`. Do not edit by hand: change the story file and run `node tools/storyboard.mjs` again.*

## How to read this

Every screen of the game is one comic panel, called a frame. Frames are listed in reading order. Each one has:

- **Shot**: the storyboard, written for an illustrator (camera, who is where, what the moment feels like, where the lettering goes).
- **Scene**: what the game draws today, in plain words: the set, the camera, who is in shot and how, and any effects.
- **Captions**: the narration boxes, read first. **Balloons**: who speaks, in order. **Sound effect**: the big lettering. A line marked *(only if …)* shows only to a reader whose choices match.
- **Then**: what the reader does next (tap Next, choose, type, pick a look, count by twos, or do a Counts lesson).

Where the reader makes a choice, each option’s frames are grouped under a **Branch** heading, and the branches meet again at the frame named after them. `{name}` is the first part of her Clan name (Moon makes Moonpaw), `{petname}` is what her Tall One calls her, and `{they}`/`{them}`/`{their}` become she/her/her or he/him/his. `{Murmur}`/`{murmur}` is the tortoiseshell’s name word: Murmur (Murmurpaw, Murmurchime, murmuring), or Mutter for a reader whose own Clan name is Murmur.

## The chapter

### f001 · panel 1

**Shot.** WIDE, FROM THE FRONT, SUNRISE, THE TAP PICTURE. The prey pile in its rows under the bramble arch in the first gold light, the back row only a dark band in the brambles’ shadow, and at the front the grizzled old tom lying flat out, fast asleep, his chin propped on a big pinecone. Our cat and Tallyheart have just come up at the other end of the rows. In play the pinecone glows softly; a tap on it rolls it out from under his chin and turns the page, and a tap anywhere else only makes him snore louder. Captions top left; the snore lettered over his head.

**Scene.** Pile: the prey pile in camp, a shady corner under an arch of brambles, the fountain’s edge at the right, in the morning (mice and voles, soft and round with their tails tucked in, all eyes shut, laid out in rows). Camera: from the front: the rows running back under the brambles (`rows`). Cast: Tallyheart (walking, kind, in the crowd, facing left); you (standing, full of wonder, lying beside the pile, facing left); the grizzled old tom (lying down, sleepy, left of the pile, facing right, eyes shut: asleep, a big pinecone under the chin, the pinecone is what she taps). Also: four rows of ten, running back under the brambles; the back row has four empty places side by side, right in its middle (three pieces, the gap, three pieces); the back row is a dark band in the brambles’ shadow: no gap, no dug earth and no “scale” can be made out; the “scale” where it was found, on the bare earth behind the back row: a small glint under the brambles. Effects: morning light, washed clean after the storm.

**Captions**

> At sunrise, the old tom is guarding the prey pile. He’s fast asleep on his pinecone.

**Sound effect:** SNNNRRRK. *(lettered where the frame says: its middle 24 across and 60 down, in hundredths of the panel)*

**Then she taps the old tom’s pinecone** (one tap, on this scene): it glows softly; a tap on it turns the page to f002; a tap anywhere else gets a small answer (lettered small beside it: “SNNNRRRK!”) and nothing more. Nothing can be got wrong, and nothing is logged. The instruction under the panel: “Tap the pinecone.” For VoiceOver, a hidden button: “Roll the pinecone.”

**Then the Counts lesson** `ch06-nines` (lives): 7 × 9, 3 × 9 (its own cats in the picture; its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry). It adapts: a 9s fact that was hard for her last time takes question 1 (never 3 × 9 or 2 × 9 or 9 × 10, either way round). Every question it asks first, and every retry, plays the two steps in its picture without a word: all ten claws lit on every cat (the hop), one curling in on each (the tuck), then unlit, and she types. A question lent to fill a gap shows the still picture. None of this frame’s own lines is said again over the first question: it is asked in the engine’s own words, and timed on itself. She types each answer on the keypad; a miss gets the sand count in two steps (two swipes for every cat, hopped by tens; then one line rubbed out of every pair, stepping back by ones) and comes back two questions later (the questions in between come from `ch05-nines`, the easiest first, never a pair asked already while there is another, each asked in that lesson’s picture and words after “One from yesterday.”). On to f006.

- Asking 3 × 9:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Three cats, nine lives each. How many lives?”
- Asking 3 × 9 again after a miss:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Here’s that one again. Three cats, nine lives each. How many lives?”
- After 3 × 9, right the first time:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Twenty-seven! Hop, then tuck.”
- After 3 × 9, right on its retry:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Twenty-seven! Hop, then tuck.”
- After a miss that is the tens (the hop without the tuck): “That’s the hop! Now the tuck: one claw in for every cat.”
- After a miss that is the tens less one (one claw tucked, for two cats or more): “So close! You tucked ONE claw. Tuck one in for every cat.”
- After a miss whose two numbers don’t make nine, once the lesson has shown her that they should (in the Training Hollow, always): “Remember: the two numbers in a nines answer make nine. Let’s scratch it out together.”
- No closing line: the next frame goes straight on.

**Then the Counts lesson** `ch06-threes` (cats): 1 × 3 (its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 3 × 2 (the first 3 lit as it is asked; its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry; its own lines after a miss), 3 × 3 (the first 6 lit as it is asked; its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry; its own lines after a miss), 3 × 5 (its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 6 × 3 (the first 15 lit as it is asked; its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a miss), 7 × 3 (the first 18 lit as it is asked; its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a miss), 3 × 8 (the first 21 lit as it is asked; its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a miss), 3 × 4 (its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 3 × 7 (its own question, kept on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry), 8 × 3 (its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry; a check: a right one never makes the fact hard). She types each answer on the keypad; a miss gets the sand count and comes back two questions later (the questions in between are the easiest of her right answers in this lesson, not the latest). ##### f056a

**Shot.** CLOSE-UP, THE DRAGONET, THEN THE COUNTS. The silver-white dragonet throws his head back with his mouth a round O and shouts the roll call into the sky; a small inset shows seven little dragonets in a row, each with three HEREs over its head. In the Counts picture the seven little dragonets take the panel, all alike and pale, three HERE!s over every head, none lit; after a miss the HEREs light a dragonet at a time as our cat hops by threes. His balloon loud, the HEREs biggest; the keypad sits below the panel.

Camera: the fox chest-up, in three-quarter view, a corner of Tallyheart in the near edge; never full face (`border-fox`). Cast: Sleet, the eldest dragonet (a Mistscale about Sprinkle’s size, silver-white with a blue-grey shade in the ridges, a paler belly, round bold eyes under bossy brows, two soft horn nubs, five frost-white claws a forepaw; never toothy) (head up, his mouth a round O: the roll call, happy, low in the long grass just past the last post, close enough to talk across it, facing left, a tuft of long grass on the head, between the horn nubs); you (sitting, full of wonder, at the leader’s left shoulder, facing right). Effects: daylight.

**Balloons**

**Then the Counts lesson** `ch06-sleet` (HEREs, little dragonets in a row, all alike and pale, three HERE!s lettered over every head): 7 × 3 (its own question, and another of its own on its retry; its own lines after a right answer; its own lines after a right retry). She types each answer on the keypad; a miss gets the set’s own picture lit a group at a time, the player keeping the count, and comes back two questions later (the questions in between come from `ch06-threes`, the easiest first, never a pair asked already while there is another, each asked as this lesson’s own question, in its picture and its voice after “A smaller roll call!”). On to f057a.

- Asking 7 × 3:
  - *Caption*: How many times does Mama hear HERE?
- Asking 7 × 3 again after a miss:
  - **Sleet**: “My roll call AGAIN! Seven of us, three HEREs each. How many HEREs?”
- After 7 × 3, right the first time:
  - **The silver-white dragon (Sleet)**: “TWENTY-ONE! You pass. Not past the post!”
- After 7 × 3, right on its retry:
  - **The silver-white dragon (Sleet)**: “TWENTY-ONE! You pass. Not past the post!”
- Before a question comes back: “My roll call AGAIN!”
- No closing line: the next frame goes straight on.

## The Case File’s cards

A piece of bark for each thing she finds out: one picture scratched in, one line, and a mark in a corner (an eye for what she saw herself, an ear for what she was only told). Each goes into her Case File at the panel that gives it, in this order:

| Card | Mark | Its line | Given at | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reed-pile` | ear | Sloshbank says ReedClan’s pile is robbed too, and left tidy. | f037 | drawn touching `tidy` from the moment she holds both: “Two piles. Both left tidy.” |
| `sleet-den` | ear | Sleet says the fox talks about ‘a fine, dry den’. | f065a | her file shows it only once foundSleet is true |
| `coil-diggers` | ear | Coil says small diggers come and go under our pile. | f097 |  |

## The book page

Title: *{name}paw’s First Moon*. This chapter’s page, under “Chapter 6: The Snake in the Stones”. Lines shown when their condition matches the reader’s choices:

- (always) On {name}paw’s fifth morning, the old tom was asleep on his pinecone, and twenty pieces were gone in five nights.
- (always) Tallyheart taught {name}paw {their} sixth Count, patrols: the threes.
- (always) On {their} first border patrol, {name}paw met Sloshbank of ReedClan, whose pile is robbed too, and left tidy.
- (if foundSleet is true) At the last post of the Barking Field, {name}paw found Sleet, the eldest dragonet, spying on the fox. Sleet heard the fox talk about a fine, dry den.
- (always) Under the Old Bridge, Coil the snake traded a secret for some quiet: small diggers come and go under the pile every night.
- (always) At sunset, Tallyheart counted out eighteen guards, six patrols of three. On the first watch, nothing happened at all.
- (always) That night {name}paw dreamed of a starry cat on the Sky River, who told {them} to count what’s missing, and then ask who was there to see it.
- (no dream typed) {name}paw’s dream that night was as quiet as the first watch.

**A dragonet page:** Sleet (`sleet`), found in this chapter by a reader whose foundSleet is true (the page is there only then). Her book gains a page for Sleet (drawn his chest puffed out, a grass seed falling off it), with room for her own drawing, beside the clutch still to find (silhouettes, seven dragonets in all):

> Silver-white, the eldest, and in charge of EVERYBODY. He does the roll call.
>
> {name}paw found him at the last post of the Barking Field, spying on the fox from the long grass.
>
> He says five, and that he’s in charge. Five more claws, counted.
